source.title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production

accepted.question_text: How should models and analyses of neutrino charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) scattering on carbon explain the apparent tension between MiniBooNE, which measured larger CCQE-like cross sections around 1 GeV, and NOMAD, which measured axial-mass values closer to deuterium at energies above 3 GeV? In particular, determine whether multinucleon (np-nh or two-particle–two-hole) effects are energy dependent and smaller at NOMAD energies, and whether NOMAD’s topological and kinematic event selections removed events whose kinematics or proton multiplicity were distorted by multinucleon dynamics.

evidence.quote:
Analysis of CCQE interactions at MiniBooNE with energies around
∼ 1 GeV on carbon indicated that the absolute diﬀerential cross sections were
consistent not only with the harder Q2 distribution implied by higher values of
MA∼ 1.35 GeV, but also with the absolute rate [15]. At around the same time,
NOMAD reported measurements of CCQE interactions on a carbon target at
higher energies ( > 3 GeV) on carbon, which resulted in MA values closer to
those obtained on deuterium (1.06±0.06 GeV/c2) [16].

One issue is the energy dependence of the additional processes and whether
one would in fact expect multi-nucleon eﬀects to be smaller at the higher
neutrino energies probed by NOMAD. Currently, the RPA-based approaches
have diﬃculty in extrapolating to higher neutrino energy, so further the-
oretical process is needed to answer this question.
On the experimental side, another issue is whether the topological and
kinematic requirements in the NOMAD selections remove events where
multi-nucleon eﬀects signiﬁcantly distort the kinematics or result in higher
proton multiplicity.

accepted.question_text: How can neutrino-nucleus CCQE-like interaction models that reproduce outgoing charged-lepton kinematics also assign a hadronic final state consistently, including outgoing proton multiplicities and kinematics, for fine-grained tracking detectors and liquid-argon time projection chambers?
accepted.context_brief: Hadronic final states in CCQE-like models

evidence.quote:
While impressive agreement is achieved in the outgoing lepton kinematics
observed in the MiniBooNE CCQE data by the RPA-based calculations,
the ability to predict the corresponding hadronic component of the inter-
action remains a challenge. With availability of data from ﬁne grained
detectors (NOMAD, MINERvA, ND280) and LAr TPCs capable of re-
solving the detailed ﬁnal state of CCQE interactions (ArgoNeuT, Micro-
BooNE), including outgoing proton multiplicities and kinematics, it will
be important to ﬁnd a suitable means of consistently assigning a predicted
hadronic state with the lepton kinematics in an event.

From the various theoretical approaches presented at the workshop, there
seems to be convergence on the characterization of the multi-nucleon eﬀects in
the inclusive CCQE process, where the process is considered integrating over
possible hadronic ﬁnal states. However, the current and upcoming suite of neu-
trino experiments utilizing ﬁne grained tracking detectors and LAr-TPCs will
demand a more exclusive description of the CCQE process in order to inter-
pret their data.

accepted.question_text: What measurements, beam-line monitoring, and common simulation practices are needed for accelerator neutrino experiments to reduce absolute neutrino flux uncertainties below 5%, including uncertainties from secondary and tertiary hadron interactions, proton-beam optics, beam-line alignment, and the approximately 20% differences among NuMI-based flux predictions?

evidence.quote:
The resulting ﬂux predictions diﬀer by as much as
20%. In order to fully proﬁt from the measurements in these experiments,
it is important to understand how these diﬀerences arise and to have a
common understanding of the methods and resulting systematic uncer-
tainties.

Continued eﬀorts to improve the neutrino ﬂux estimates will certainly
produce additional dividends. Eﬀective use of hadron production mea-
surements is essential, but likely insuﬃcient, to achieve better than 5%
uncertainty on the predicted absolute ﬂux, where eﬀects of secondary and
tertiary interactions, and uncertainties related to the primary proton beam
optics, beam line alignment, etc. may become signiﬁcant, possibly dom-
inant, sources of systematic uncertainty once the primary production is
measured precisely.

accepted.question_text: How can the scaling analyses and short-range correlation information obtained from inclusive electron quasielastic scattering be made usable in neutrino-nucleus CCQE analyses, given that neutrino experiments generally do not know the incident neutrino energy event by event and therefore cannot directly establish the transferred momentum q and transferred energy ω?

evidence.quote:
Clearly a great deal relevant to neutrino–nucleus scattering has been learned
via the scaling analyses of inclusive electron QE scattering from nuclei. Such
measurements are feasible with electrons where the critical variablesq and ω are
readily obtained from measurement of the momentum of the scattered electron.
Unfortunately, for most neutrino experiments these quantities are out of reach.
Thus, scaling cannot at the moment be applied to neutrino experiments due to a
lack of knowledge of the incident neutrino energy which limits how well q and ω
can be established.

The appearance of short-range (high momentum) pairwise
correlations among 20% of the nucleons in a nucleus is especially important.
These correlations are known to be the cause of the enhancement appearing
in the nuclear transverse response. These correlations will be shown to be
important in neutrino-nucleus CCQE scattering.

accepted.question_text: In Random Phase Approximation (RPA) models of neutrino-nucleus scattering that reproduce MiniBooNE CCQE-like data, what theoretically justified treatment should be used for the transverse magnetic and axial responses, conservation of the vector current, and non-plane-wave hadronic final states, instead of assuming that the transverse magnetic and axial responses are identical and representing all hadronic states as plane waves?

evidence.quote:
transverse magnetic and axial responses are identical. There is no obvious justi-
ﬁcation for this apart from the similarity of a non-relativistic reduction of their
associated operators (( ⃗ σ× q/|q|)τ±). The eﬀects of pion exchange on vector
and axial vector currents are known [72, 73] to be quite diﬀerent
While very successful in reproducing the MiniBooNE data, it is not clear
that this approach is robust. The weak current employed by Martini et al. is
one-body so it is not clear to what degree conservation of the vector current
is respected. Furthermore, all hadronic states are represented as plane-waves,
which is certainly not correct and requires taming some two body integrals that
would otherwise be inﬁnite [74].

accepted.question_text: Why do the Martini and IFIC/Nieves RPA-based calculations for carbon neutrino CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux give a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution that differs by about a factor of two, and is the unresolved axial-response enhancement responsible for this difference?

evidence.quote:
Of note is the large diﬀerence between their calculation and that
from Martini et al. in the contribution from 2p−2h conﬁgurations.

...however our 2p2h contribution is
about a factor of 2 smaller!
J. Nieves, IFIC, CSIC & University of V alencia

Such enhancement is still an issue under investigation. In
the presentation of the RPA formalism and results, terms such as “ n-particle,
n-hole” ﬁnal states are often used, creating some confusion withn-body currents
employed in other formalisms.

accepted.question_text: What is the physical origin, magnitude, and model dependence of the axial transverse response enhancement from two-body currents in neutrino-nucleus quasielastic scattering, and how should theoretical frameworks such as RPA, Relativistic Mean Field (RMF), and superscaling (SuSA) state and test their assumptions about vector and axial transverse enhancements when predicting CCQE cross sections?

evidence.quote:
More surprising is the enhanced axial response, not explicit in the Sxx and
Sxy of Figure 28, but clearly present in Figure 29. The enhancement of the
axial response is sizable and present at all three-momentum transfers and given
its role in the coherent transverse interference response ( Sxy), it is clear that its
neglect leads to seriously under predicting the NCQE and CCQE cross sections
on carbon.

The origin of this two-body
current enhancement in the case of the axial response has not yet been identiﬁed
by the authors.

At the workshop, we saw various approaches
as to whether there is a corresponding enhancement in the axial response,
and indications from ab initio methods that such an enhancement is indeed
present. It is critical to better understand this situation fundamentally
(i.e. what is the nature and magnitude of this enhancement) and to
clarify within each theoretical framework (RPA, RMF, SuSA, etc.) what
assumptions were made with regard to these enhancements in calculating
the CCQE cross section.

accepted.question_text: How can nonrelativistic ab initio nuclear approaches such as Green’s Function Monte Carlo calculations, which are currently limited to light nuclei, be extended or connected to the relativistic momentum and energy transfers encountered in accelerator neutrino beams so that they contribute to a complete CCQE description?
accepted.context_brief: Relativistic extension of ab initio calculations

evidence.quote:
They employ a pa-
rameterized version of the nucleon-nucleon interaction (VA18), including 3-body
forces (TNI), and solve for the low-lying states of the nucleus using quantum
Green’s Function Monte Carlo (GFMC) techniques. The computational com-
plexity of such an approach is currently limited to light nuclei ( A≤ 12).

The approach of the NUCLEI collaboration is necessarily non-relativistic
and serious questions were raised at the workshop as to how to extend this
work to the momentum and energy transfers encountered with neutrino beams

While there are domains where a non-relativistic treatment may suﬃce,
it is clear that a complete picture of the CCQE process will require a
thorough accounting of relativistic eﬀects.

accepted.question_text: How should Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) and Relativistic Green’s Function (RGF) approaches be constrained so that the many-body physics apparently captured through final-state interactions and relativistic optical potentials is understood, the choice of optical potential is no longer ambiguous, and the enhancement of CCQE cross sections can be reconciled with multinucleon emission and other non-nucleonic contributions?

evidence.quote:
It is certainly surprising that so much apparently complex physics contained
in the GFMC approach can be captured in the ﬁnal state interactions of the
outgoing nucleon with an appropriate RMF. While there is presently appreciable
latitude in determining the appropriate RMF to apply in a particular case, it
clearly is of interest and importance to better understand the RMF approach
to remove this ambiguity and establish contact with the relevant underlying
physics.

The larger cross sections in the RGF model
arise from the translation to the inclusive strength of the
overall effect of inelastic channels. At present, lacking a
phenomenological optical potential which exactly fulﬁlls
the dispersion relations in the whole energy region of
interest, the RGF prediction is not univocally determined
from the elastic phenomenology, although some preference
to the EDAI predictions should be given.

to
clarify the content of the enhancement of the CCQE cross
sections obtained in the RGF model compared to those of
the IA models, a careful evaluation of all nuclear effects
and of the relevance of multinucleon emission and of some
non-nucleonic contributions [ 27] is required.

accepted.question_text: How should oscillation analyses reconstruct the incident neutrino energy in CCQE-like events when only the outgoing lepton or an incomplete hadronic final state is measured, given Fermi motion, scattering from correlated nucleon pairs, finite detection thresholds, limited neutron detection, flux uncertainties, and model-dependent multinucleon effects that can bias the mapping between true and reconstructed energy?

evidence.quote:
From this body of work, it is clear that the extracted distribution of incident
neutrino energies for a given measured charged lepton momentum greatly de-
pends on the energy distribution of the incident neutrino ﬂux, which typically
has signiﬁcant uncertainties. If it were possible to measure the energy of all
the ﬁnal state particles, in addition to the outgoing lepton, it would be possible
in principle to unambiguously assign a neutrino energy by exploiting energy
conservation. Practically, all detectors have ﬁnite energy thresholds for particle
detection and other limitations ( e.g. detection of ﬁnal state neutrons) that will
induce errors that depend on the accuracy of the underlying physics models.

Using the momentum of the
ﬁnal state muon to infer the incident neutrino energy can greatly underestimate
that energy if the muon was produced by CCQE scattering oﬀ a neutron in a
correlated pair. The correlated pair can be viewed as being far oﬀ-shell and the
scattering interaction must put both nucleons back on-shell.

However, a wider range of models need to be explored, and as the
precision of the measurement increases as more data is accumulated at T2K, a
more detailed analysis will be necessary.

accepted.question_text: What useful and reliable treatment of final-state interactions (FSI)—the propagation of hadrons created at the electroweak vertex through the nuclear medium—can be incorporated into neutrino event generators for exclusive CCQE final states, given that a fully formal treatment would require many unknown form factors and current generator implementations show shortcomings in proton-emission observables?

evidence.quote:
Final state interactions (FSI), the interactions of the hadrons created at the
electroweak vertex as they traverse the nuclear medium, must be accounted for if
one is to understand the exclusive ﬁnal states that arise from the CCQE process.

Formally, a full treatment of FSI requires, among other things, the intro-
duction of a very large number of new and unknown form factors; this has not
happened to date, and is not likely to happen in the future. However, the
possibility of employing large ﬁne-grained tracking detectors and LAr-TPCs in
neutrino experiments has greatly increased the interest in improving the FSI
treatment in neutrino event generators.

It is generally recognized that FSI present a very serious challenge to theory if
a useful and reliable procedure is to be developed and incorporated into neutrino
event generators. It appears progress on this front will require substantial input
from electron scattering and that GiBUU (as one example) will be a useful tool
to digest such data and to connect it to neutrino scattering.

accepted.question_text: What remaining neutral-current single-photon production mechanisms, especially anomalous ωZγ contributions with large theoretical uncertainties, and what direct measurements by MicroBooNE, MINERvA, ND280/T2K, or similar detectors are needed to make this background sufficiently controlled for electron-neutrino appearance studies?

evidence.quote:
Overall, the situation for neutrino NC γ production seems to be converging
and under control. The theoretical models agree with the experimentally de-
termined predictions for this process as determined by MiniBooNE. However,
there are possible contributions, namely from the anomalous ωZγ term, where
theoretical uncertainties remain large and the calculation is not robust.

of the overall importance to νe appearance studies, the issue is not completely
closed and we should keep a close eye on possible future theoretical or experi-
mental advances.

Following a search for this process at
NOMAD in a relatively high energy neutrino beam, we can look forward to
further experimental study of this process with LAr-TPCs such as MicroBooNE.
MINERvA and ND280 at T2K could also provide measurements of this process.

accepted.question_text: How can computationally sophisticated neutrino-nucleus calculations, including RPA differential cross-section tables, precomputed hadronic tensors, and possibly Green’s Function Monte Carlo results, be delivered to neutrino event generators together with uncertainty estimates and exclusive-final-state guidance so experiments can confront the predictions with data?

evidence.quote:
However, it is unreasonable to even contemplate directly incorporating
some of the methods presented at the workshop (e.g. a Green’s Function Monte
Carlo calculation) into an event generator, and thus the results of such calcula-
tions must be provided more directly from the theorists to the event generator.

Some new methods were already in place at the workshop, where tables of diﬀer-
ential cross sections from RPA calculations were directly inserted into an event
generator, while new ideas, such as precomputing the hadronic tensor from such
a calculation, emerged from the discussions. This is an interface which will have
to be actively maintained by the experimental and theoretical community in or-
der to facilitate the incorporation of new theoretical predictions into the event
generators, a necessary step to enable a robust confrontation of these predictions
with experimental data.

First, new calculations must be provided in a form that can be incor-
porated into a neutrino event generator so that the results can be used
by neutrino experiments. Experimentalists will require guidance in esti-
mating the uncertainties in the prediction in order to use it eﬀectively in
an analysis. Finally, experiments will need predictions on the exclusive
ﬁnal states of neutrino-induced CCQE interactions.

accepted.question_text: How should neutrino experiments report CCQE measurements with precise definitions of the event selection, observables, and the meaning of “CCQE,” while providing model-independent quantities and flux information that theorists can calculate directly, so that comparisons with neutrino and electron-scattering theory are unambiguous?

evidence.quote:
It is essential to reduce any barrier between the reported measurements
and the quantities that can be predicted from theory. There has already
been signiﬁcant progress in moving from measurements of eﬀective param-
eters to more model-independent quantities that can be directly calculated
by theorists with neutrino ﬂux predictions provided by experimentalists.
It will be critical for all experimental eﬀorts to engage and continuously
develop this interface in order to provide theorists with the most eﬀective
input.

We have seen that precisely deﬁning what is meant by “CCQE” in a
measurement is critical for interpreting the results. Clarity in the event
selection and observables will become even more important as engagement
continues with theorists and the electron scattering community, where
terms such as “quasi-elastic scattering” and “ﬁnal state interactions” may
mean something substantially diﬀerent.
